title: FACIAL CLEFTING, OBLIQUE, 1
alt_titles: OCULOMAXILLOFACIAL DYSPLASIA WITH OBLIQUE FACIAL CLEFTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that oblique facial clefting-1 (OBLFC1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPECC1L gene on chromosome 22q11.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefting-1 (OBLFC1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPECC1L gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We show that loss-of-function mutations in SPECC1L are pathogenic for this human developmental disorder
checks.explanation: Abstract states SPECC1L loss-of-function mutations cause ObFC but does not specify heterozygosity (abstract only).

checks.claim: The SPECC1L gene is located on chromosome 22q11.
checks.evidence_quote: Deficiency of the cytoskeletal protein SPECC1L leads to oblique facial clefting.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature restating the gene; the abstract itself does not mention 22q11.

paragraphs.text: Oblique facial clefts are rare, severe craniofacial malformations. The clefts run obliquely from the upper lip or mouth region toward the eye (corresponding to Tessier clefts in the oro-orbital/naso-ocular region). They may involve the lip, maxilla, nose, and the inferior eyelid and orbit. They may occur on one side or both, and they can occur with other malformations. Most cases are sporadic.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts are rare craniofacial malformations.
checks.evidence_quote: Chromosomal studies should be performed in children with such rare malformations.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls oblique facial clefts rare malformations.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts are severe craniofacial malformations.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 4 cited papers. Severity not mentioned in abstract.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts run obliquely from the upper lip or mouth region toward the eye.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 4 cited papers. Cleft course not described in abstract.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts correspond to Tessier clefts in the oro-orbital/naso-ocular region.
checks.evidence_quote: Oblique facial clefts are rare and include types 2-6 of Tessier's classification.
checks.explanation: The abstract links the clefts to Tessier types 2-6 but does not mention an 'oro-orbital/naso-ocular region'.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts may involve the lip, maxilla, nose, and the inferior eyelid and orbit.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 4 cited papers. Involved structures not described in abstract.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts may be unilateral or bilateral.
checks.evidence_quote: An eight month old girl was born with symmetrical bilateral oblique facial clefts and calcaneovarus foot deformity.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes one bilateral case. It does not mention that the clefts can also occur on one side only.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefts can occur together with other malformations.
checks.evidence_quote: An eight month old girl was born with symmetrical bilateral oblique facial clefts and calcaneovarus foot deformity. CT scan of the head showed severe bilateral ocular hypoplasia
checks.explanation: The patient had the clefts together with a foot deformity and ocular hypoplasia.

checks.claim: Most cases of oblique facial clefting are sporadic.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 4 cited papers. Sporadic occurrence not mentioned in abstract.

paragraphs.text: The heterozygous SPECC1L mutations reported by Saadi et al. (2011) are consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Most cases have been sporadic.

checks.claim: The heterozygous SPECC1L mutations reported by Saadi et al. (2011) in oblique facial clefting are consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.
checks.explanation: Abstract does not mention heterozygosity or inheritance mode.

checks.claim: Most cases of oblique facial clefting have been sporadic.
checks.explanation: Sporadic cases not mentioned in abstract.

paragraphs.text: Saadi et al. (2011) studied a patient with oblique facial clefting who carried a de novo balanced chromosomal translocation. The breakpoint on chromosome 22q11 disrupted the SPECC1L gene, which pointed to SPECC1L as a candidate gene for the disorder.

checks.claim: Saadi et al. (2011) studied a patient with oblique facial clefting who carried a de novo balanced chromosomal translocation.
checks.explanation: No translocation patient described in abstract; may be in full text.

checks.claim: In a patient with oblique facial clefting studied by Saadi et al. (2011), the translocation breakpoint on chromosome 22q11 disrupted the SPECC1L gene.
checks.explanation: Translocation breakpoint at 22q11 not mentioned in abstract.

checks.claim: Disruption of SPECC1L by a translocation breakpoint in a patient with oblique facial clefting identified SPECC1L as a candidate gene for the disorder.
checks.explanation: Candidate-gene identification via translocation not mentioned in abstract.

paragraphs.text: Saadi et al. (2011) went on to screen SPECC1L in a cohort of patients with oblique facial clefts. They identified heterozygous missense mutations in SPECC1L in 2 patients. Functional studies supported a role for SPECC1L in craniofacial development. In zebrafish, knockdown of the ortholog caused defects in facial cartilage. In cultured cells, SPECC1L deficiency affected the actin cytoskeleton and cell migration. Saadi et al. (2011) proposed that SPECC1L is needed for the facial processes to fuse properly, through its role in cell adhesion and migration.

checks.claim: Saadi et al. (2011) screened the SPECC1L gene in a cohort of patients with oblique facial clefts.
checks.explanation: Cohort screening not described in abstract.

checks.claim: Saadi et al. (2011) identified heterozygous missense mutations in SPECC1L in 2 patients with oblique facial clefts.
checks.explanation: Abstract mentions loss-of-function mutations but gives no patient count, zygosity, or missense type.

checks.claim: Functional studies by Saadi et al. (2011) supported a role for SPECC1L in craniofacial development.
checks.evidence_quote: SPECC1L is a critical organizer of vertebrate facial morphogenesis
checks.explanation: Functional data in zebrafish, mouse, Drosophila, and cells support role in facial development.

checks.claim: Knockdown of the SPECC1L ortholog in zebrafish caused defects in facial cartilage.
checks.evidence_quote: In zebrafish, knockdown of a SPECC1L homolog produces a faceless phenotype with loss of jaw and facial structures
checks.explanation: Abstract describes loss of jaw and facial structures, not specifically facial cartilage defects.

checks.claim: SPECC1L deficiency in cultured cells affected the actin cytoskeleton.
checks.evidence_quote: its deficiency results in defective actin-cytoskeleton reorganization, as well as abnormal cell adhesion and migration
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: SPECC1L deficiency in cultured cells affected cell migration.
checks.evidence_quote: its deficiency results in defective actin-cytoskeleton reorganization, as well as abnormal cell adhesion and migration
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Saadi et al. (2011) proposed that SPECC1L is required for proper fusion of the facial processes through its role in cell adhesion and migration.
checks.evidence_quote: Collectively, these data demonstrate that SPECC1L functions in actin-cytoskeleton reorganization and is required for proper facial morphogenesis.
checks.explanation: Abstract concludes SPECC1L required for facial morphogenesis and notes primordia fuse, but does not explicitly propose fusion via adhesion/migration.
